Let's load the document that we will be working with:

```{r}

library(readxl)

usdata <- read_xlsx("C:/Users/artem/Desktop/R/Programación R/US Statistics.xlsx")

# Change the location of the document by YOUR location of the document using CTRL C + CTRL V

usdata <- as.data.frame(usdata)

```

Please, note that the previous code may fail to execute if the library `readxl` is not installed.

You can install the library by writing down in the console:

install.packages("readxl)

(This same logic applies to any other library or libraries that may be needed.)

### The R Base Package

"This package contains the basic functions which let R function as a language: arithmetic, input/output, basic programming support, etc. Its contents are available through inheritance from any environment."

Check (write) in console:

library(help = "base")

With base R, we can get:

* An overview of the structure of the data:

```{r}

str(usdata)

```

* Class of the data

```{r}

class(usdata)

```

* Class of an individual column (variable):

```{r}

class(usdata$`Unadjusted Depreciation Estimates`)

```

* The length of the vector:

```{r}

length(usdata$`Adjusted Business Profits`)

```

* The number of the rows and the number of the columns:

```{r}

nrow(usdata)
ncol(usdata)

```

* The names of the columns that we have in the dataset:

```{r}

names(usdata)

```

* The number of unique registers:

```{r}

unique(usdata)

unique(usdata$`Unadjusted Depreciation Estimates`)

```

* The arithmetic mean:

```{r}

mean(usdata$`Unadjusted Business Profits`)

```

* The minimum and maximum values:

```{r}

min(usdata$`Adjusted Depreciation Estimates`)

max(usdata$`Adjusted Depreciation Estimates`)

```

* Check if there are NA values:

```{r}

is.na(usdata)

sum(is.na(usdata))

```

* Round the arithmetic results:

```{r}

round(usdata$`Adjusted Depreciation Estimates`, digits = 2)

#Rounding to 2 digits

```

* Subset a register as per some criterion:

```{r}

usdata[usdata$Year >= "1929" & usdata$Year <= "1934", ] 

#Remember to add a coma when performing a row-wise transformation

#We add a coma in the beginning when the transformation is column-wise

```


As can be seen, base R allows us to perform a wide selection of useful operations.

However, for a more professional and an even wider selection of operations, we shall turn to:

### Tidyverse

"At a high level, the tidyverse is a language for solving data science challenges with R code. Its primary goal is to facilitate a conversation between a human and a computer about data. Less abstractly, the tidyverse is a collection of R packages that share a high-level design philosophy and low-level grammar and data structures, so that learning one package makes it easier to learn the next."

https://tidyverse.org/

Tidyverse is a broad collection of packages for data science, that include `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `lubridate`, `ggplot2`, `forcats`, and others.

As for now, we will stick to commands contained in `dplyr` and `tidyr`.

For convenience, it is useful to load tidyverse instead of each separate package.

Tidyverse relies crucially on the pipe |> operator:

```{r}

# |> 
  
# ON WINDOWS: Control + Shift + M
  
# ON MAC: ⌘ + Shift + M

```

When using the pipe, the logic is as follows:

0. Make sure that the library is loaded: `library(tidyverse)` .

1. Write the name of the dataset.

2. Use the shortcut for the pipe operator on the right side after it.

3. Go to the next line, making sure that the indentation (space) is respected.

4. Write the specific command that you wish to use.


Thus, some of the main commands are:

## select

```{r}

library(tidyverse)

usdata |> 
  select(c(Year, `Unadjusted Business Profits`, `Unadjusted Depreciation Estimates`))

#We perform a selection of 3 columns

#The letter "c" is to indicate that this is a vector (two or more variables together)

```

If we wish to select the results, all that we have to do is to create a new variable and perform the required assignation (using either <- or = ):

```{r}

usdata_selection = usdata |> 
  select(c(Year, `Unadjusted Business Profits`, `Unadjusted Depreciation Estimates`))

```


## filter

```{r}

usdata |> 
  filter(Year >= "1929" & Year <= "1939") |> 
  filter(`Adjusted Business Profits` < "0")

# Notice how we can "enlarge" the pipe by adding additional criteria

```

Of course, we can combine the previous command in a single pipeline:

```{r}

usdata |> 
  filter(Year >= "1929" & Year <= "1939" & `Adjusted Business Profits` < "0") |> 
  select(c(Year, `Adjusted Business Profits`, `Adjusted Depreciation Estimates`))

```

## glimpse

```{r}

glimpse(usdata)

#This is a direct command for an overview of the dataset

```

## arrange (in ascending or descending order)

```{r}

usdata |> 
  arrange(`Adjusted Business Profits`)

#Arranging in ascending order

```

```{r}

usdata |> 
  arrange(desc(`Adjusted Business Profits`))

#Arranging in descending order

```

## mutate (create, modify, and/or delete columns)

```{r}

usdata |> 
  mutate(NetBusinessGrowth = `Unadjusted Business Profits` - `Unadjusted Depreciation Estimates`)

```

## transmute (create, modify, and / or delete columns containing only the specified computations, and nothing else)

```{r}

usdata |> 
  transmute(NetBusinessGrowth = `Unadjusted Business Profits` - `Unadjusted Depreciation Estimates`)

```

## rename

```{r}

usdata |> 
  rename("Time" = Year)

```

## summarise

```{r}

usdata |> 
  summarise(MeanOfAdjustedBusinessProfits = mean(`Adjusted Business Profits`))

```

Finally, with the knowledge of the previous commands, we can think of constructing a whole pipeline:

```{r}

usdata_pipeline = usdata |> 
  filter(Year >= "1929" & Year <="1939") |> 
  select(c(Year, `Adjusted Business Profits`, `Adjusted Depreciation Estimates`)) |> 
  mutate(NetBusinessGrowth = `Adjusted Business Profits` - `Adjusted Depreciation Estimates`) |> 
  rename("YearSelected" = Year) |> 
  arrange(desc(NetBusinessGrowth))

```
